detail:
You Might Be Able to Invest in the Starlab Space Station -- but Should You?
Rich Smith, The Motley Fool

LDOS
NOC

After more than a quarter-century in service, the International Space Station is ready for its last hurrah. Sometime after 2030, the space agency plans to pay Elon Musk's SpaceX $850 million to push ISS out of orbit and into the ocean. It's sad news -- but here's the good news:

America is building a new international space station, this time owned and operated by private companies -- private international companies -- to replace ISS. Several teams are competing for the honor, with pole position likely held by Starlab, a consortium led by Voyager Technologies (NYSE: VOYG) and including partners such as Hilton Worldwide, Leidos, Northrop Grumman, and Palantir.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

And now here's (potentially) the best part: You may be able to invest in Starlab directly.

Image source: Getty Images.
How to buy a space station in three easy steps

Rumors are circulating regarding an effort to raise $300 million in "Series A" funding for the Starlab joint venture. Series A is the term of art for the first major funding round after a start-up company has exhausted its "seed capital" financing. Multiple institutional investors have already confirmed they're contributing capital to the funding round. If you're looking for an opportunity to get in on the "ground floor" of a space station company -- this may be it.

But "getting in" might not be easy. To participate in Starlab's funding round (assuming it happens), you first need to find a private investment company that has been invited to participate. I personally know of one such company, but don't have permission to name it publicly -- so I won't. (But it is out there.)

Next, you need to find out the price.

Starlab is seeking to raise $300 million by selling "preferred units" (not exactly stock, but similar) in the joint venture. Each unit is reportedly valued near $90,000, and the company as a whole is valued at $950 million prior to the Series A (and could be worth $1.25 billion afterward).

Finally, you should decide if that price is "worth it."

Should you invest (if you can)?

For me, that's the real question, because I'm not convinced investing directly in the Starlab joint venture is the best route -- even if that's an option for you.

Consider: Starlab has received $211 million in grant funding from NASA, and a further $15 million from the Texas Space Commission, plus tens of millions in capital contributions from several of its joint venture partners. But according to the latest data from S&P Global Market Intelligence, Starlab has no revenue -- much less profit -- yet. That's not surprising, seeing as the joint venture hasn't yet built or launched the space station it needs to generate the revenue -- but it does raise the risk of investing in Starlab.

What Will a $10,000 Investment in Palantir Be Worth by 2030?
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool

PLTR
^GSPC
NVDA

Palantir (NASDAQ: PLTR) investors have had a fairly rocky 2026. For most of the year, the stock was losing money. However, starting in August, Palantir reversed the decline and has now gained about 12% for the year. That is roughly in line with the gain for the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC).

However, if you survey the average Palantir investor, almost all of them will say that beating the market is their long-term priority for holding Palantir shares. So, 2026 has been a disappointing year so far. But as long-term investors, there is still plenty of time to deliver strong returns.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

So, if you invested $10,000 into Palantir now, what could that be worth by 2030? And will it be good enough to beat the market? Let's take a look.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
Palantir's AI business is booming

Palantir originally started off offering its AI platform to government entities. This was an incredibly popular offering, and Palantir's government contracts still make up the majority of its revenue stream today. However, Palantir also expanded to the commercial side of the business, and it's seeing huge adoption of its AI platform.

Essentially, Palantir is an AI platform that plugs into existing data streams and helps derive actionable insights. Through automation, Palantir can also assist in deploying AI agents that do tasks on behalf of its users. Palantir's platform dramatically improves the efficiency of one person in their role and can provide decision-making capabilities that far exceed what a human can deliver.

Companies and governments are adopting Palantir's software at a breathtaking pace, which is evidenced by its 93% revenue growth rate in Q2. U.S. commercial revenue grew even faster, with revenue from this segment increasing at a 149% pace. AI adoption is happening rapidly, and Palantir is one of the companies that's taking market share.

One of the biggest surprises with Palantir is how great its margins are. New headlines are filled with stories about how quickly some AI firms are growing, but also highlight that they're spending far more than they make. Palantir isn't in that boat, as it delivered an impressive 55% profit margin in Q2.

It doesn't get better than that, but this also opens up a new problem.

Palantir's stock is pricey

Palantir's stock is one of the more expensive on the market, and it trades for almost 125 times this year's earnings.

title: Palantir stock faces brutal test after crushing expectations
detail:
Palantir stock faces brutal test after crushing expectations
Faizan Farooque, Celine Provini
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 9:47 PM EDT 7 min read
PLTR
Trade PLTR on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) has created a problem most companies would love to have: Wall Street now expects it to crush expectations.

MarketBeat expects $2.18 billion in revenue and 41 cents per share from the AI software company's third-quarter results after the market closes Nov. 2. Revenue would increase 84% year over year.

Palantir's own prediction is less optimistic. Wall Street has successfully factored another beat into its expectations ahead of the report, as management guided for $2.160 billion to $2.164 billion in sales.

This disparity contributes to the explanation of an odd division among experts.

Citi raised its Palantir price target to $250 from $245 on Oct. 22 and expects U.S. commercial revenue to grow more than 140%, according to TipRanks.

But Investing.com, citing StoneX, reported that the firm maintained a Hold rating, even as it also expected a strong quarter. StoneX said investors may focus less on whether Palantir beats estimates than on how large the upside is.

Both companies anticipate Palantir's success. The point of contention is how much positive news investors should already anticipate.

Palantir's growth has made a beat the baseline

Investors have several reasons to expect even better results from Palantir.

Second-quarter revenue surged 93% year over year to $1.94 billion, while U.S. commercial revenue jumped 149% to $764 million. U.S. government revenue rose 90% to $809 million.

The company also closed 220 deals worth at least $1 million during the quarter, including 98 worth at least $5 million and 73 worth at least $10 million.

With adjusted free cash flow of $1.22 billion, the margin was 63%.

Palantir reported that U.S. commercial residual deal value, or contractual work that hasn't yet been recorded as revenue, increased 124% to $6.24 billion.

These figures complicate the value argument beyond just labeling Palantir as pricey.

Investors often expect that the company's growth will ultimately support an exceptionally high stock-market value. However, every extraordinary quarter also complicates the subsequent comparison.

Palantir raised its full-year revenue guidance after the second quarter to $8.150 billion to $8.158 billion, representing roughly 82% growth. It also expects U.S. commercial revenue to exceed $3.424 billion, or grow at least 134%.

Despite increasingly challenging year-earlier comparisons, Citi now anticipates that business will expand by more than 140% in the third quarter.

Citi's checks with Palantir partners showed strong demand across U.S. commercial and government businesses, according to TipRanks.

What Happened?

Palantir Technologies (PLTR:NASDAQ) told Reuters on October 21 that no one can switch off the AI system used by NATO's military headquarters, Palantir included. "There are no kill switches," said Louis Mosley, executive vice president for the UK and Europe, adding that whether Palantir staff help operate the Maven Smart System is up to the customer. Shares fell 2.74% to $196.19 on October 22, the day the report ran, as chip and AI infrastructure stocks also sold off. No outlet confirmed a Palantir-specific cause for the drop.

The pledge is the company's assurance, not an independent technical review. It also speaks to the sharpest critique of how Palantir sells: that customers end up dependent on its engineers.

Gartner Says Engineer-Built AI Gets Abandoned. Palantir's Costs Disagree, So Far

Palantir pairs its software with forward-deployed engineers, staff embedded at customer sites. On September 29, Gartner predicted that 70% of enterprises will abandon agentic AI built by vendor forward-deployed engineering by 2028, as costs climb and customers struggle to change the systems themselves. Gartner did not name Palantir.

The second quarter points the other way. CFO Dave Glazer reported adjusted expense, which excludes stock-based compensation, of $741 million, up 37% year over year, while revenue grew 93%. If every new deployment needed proportionally more engineers, costs would grow in step with revenue, not at less than half its pace.

Palantir EBIT & Margins (TIKR)

Palantir's October 21 customer update offered one example. McCarthy Building Companies, which runs Palantir's Foundry and AIP, delivered better-than-frontier performance at significantly lower cost with a post-trained open-weight model, saving 30,000 hours a year, according to the release.

Europe Is Where the Control Question Bites

Germany and France have not adopted Maven for their own armed forces, citing concerns about relying on a U.S. company, according to Reuters, and Starlink disruptions in Ukraine have sharpened that worry. The growth gap predates the scare. In 2025, U.S. revenue grew 74.7% to $3.32 billion, UK revenue grew 40.3% to $427 million, and rest-of-world revenue grew 10.2% to $728 million. In Q2, international commercial revenue rose just 2% from Q1 (26% year over year), to $182 million.

Palantir Guided for $2.16 Billion in Revenue for Q3. Its Last 2 Quarters Suggest We Should Expect More.
Patrick Sanders, The Motley Fool
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 12:24 PM EDT 5 min read
PLTR
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR) has been one of the biggest winners of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, with its stock gaining more than 1,000% over the last three years. But investors who think the company's best days are behind it may be in for a surprise when Palantir reports its third-quarter results on Nov. 2.

That's because Palantir has developed a habit of beating its own revenue guidance -- and its margins are widening.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The company's guidance was for third-quarter revenue between $2.160 billion and $2.164 billion, which would amount to another impressive quarter of growth. But based on Palantir's performances in the first half of the year, I think that forecast is far too conservative.

In fact, I wouldn't be surprised if Palantir delivers more than $2.3 billion in revenue, easily surpassing its own expectations.

Here's why.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
Palantir keeps raising the bar

Palantir has been on an incredible run this year, fueled by demand for its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP), which helps businesses and government agencies analyze enormous amounts of information and use AI to make decisions.

But what's particularly interesting is how Palantir consistently underestimates its own growth. When the company issued its first-quarter guidance in February, it projected revenue between $1.532 billion and $1.536 billion. Instead, it delivered $1.633 billion -- about 6.4% above the midpoint of that range.

The second quarter's beat was even better. Management projected revenue between $1.797 billion and $1.801 billion, but Palantir generated $1.935 billion -- approximately 7.5% more than projected.

The company's growth is accelerating, too. Revenue increased 16% sequentially in the first quarter, followed by a 19% increase in the second quarter. Year-over-year revenue growth reached 93% in Q2, up from 85% in Q1.

Now look at the company's third-quarter guidance.

Palantir's forecast of approximately $2.16 billion represents sequential growth of just under 12%. That would be a significant slowdown in growth from the previous quarter.

That doesn't make much sense to me, particularly when Palantir's commercial business has been expanding so rapidly. If the company simply matches its second-quarter sequential growth rate of 19%, third-quarter revenue would reach approximately $2.3 billion. And I think there's a reasonable chance Palantir will do even better.

Palantir's new partnership with Knox Systems aims to accelerate the delivery of commercial software to federal agencies and defense customers.

Palantir shares have rallied substantially since its second-quarter earnings report, but valuation concerns remain despite strong business growth.

The company's Nov. 2 earnings report will test expectations for government revenue, commercial demand, and free cash flow.

Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR) has been revalued since its Q2 2026 earnings report. The share price is up over 55% since the report, which has set a higher floor.

But investors are wondering about the ceiling. Valuation concerns still make investors wary of overpaying, even as the company keeps outperforming. Michael Burry has been one of the most outspoken Palantir critics and has initiated a short position on PLTR.

→ Lam Research's Earnings Beat Wasn't the Real Story—Its 2027 Outlook Was

Deal flow argues in favor of the bulls. Palantir has steadily added clients to its commercial and government business units. The latter was in focus this week with the announcement of a partnership with Knox Systems. Knox runs a managed cloud built to get commercial software approved for federal use.

This partnership won't settle the valuation debate because neither company disclosed financial terms. But it strengthens Palantir's position as a central player in government software delivery, not just one vendor among many.

→ GM Beat and Added a $20 Billion Buyback—Why Did the Stock Fall?

That distinction matters with Q3 earnings expected on Nov. 2. Investors want proof that government growth can keep pace with Palantir's surging commercial business.

What the Knox Deal Means in Plain English

Selling software to the federal government is different from selling to a corporation. Agencies can only use cloud products that pass strict security reviews. The main standard is FedRAMP, the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program.

→ Is Texas Instruments Setting Up for Its Next Big Breakout?

Defense work raises the bar further. The Pentagon uses Impact Levels to rate how sensitive data is. IL5 covers sensitive, unclassified data, including unclassified national security systems. Earning these approvals often takes a year or more. That cost keeps many strong commercial products out of government hands.

Knox helps address that problem by providing access to an already-authorized cloud environment. Software makers move into Knox's cloud instead of building a compliant fortress themselves. Knox says it can deliver FedRAMP authorization in 90 days or less. It already hosts more than 100 AI and enterprise applications, including software from Adobe (NASDAQ: ADBE).
